slides: Let's continue with tables and charts.

slides.say: What's the difference between a table and a chart? A table puts related data together, in rows and columns.
We find a value where a row and a column cross. Let's take the row thirty-one to forty, and the siblings column.
They cross at two point eight. So people aged thirty-one to forty have two point eight siblings, on average.
at: They cross at two point eight

slides.say: A chart shows the same kind of data as a picture.
Think of Excel. We type the data into a table, and we click insert chart.

slides: Excel asks which kind of chart we want. Columns, a line, a pie, and more.

slides.say: We choose the chart that shows our data best. Different charts help us see different things. We'll see that in the next lessons.
Here's an important difference from geometry. In geometry, a figure is not necessarily drawn to scale.
In charts, we can read values from the drawing. But first, check the scale, the units, and any break in the axis.
Often the fastest way is just to look. On the same axes, over the same time interval, a steeper line means a bigger change.
Let's see it on this chart. It shows a score, by the number of full practice tests a student did.
At the start the line is very steep. From the first test to the fifth, the score jumps a lot.
at: From the first test to the fifth

slides.say: From about the eighth test, the line is almost flat. So the score hardly goes up any more.

slides: We saw all of this in one look, with no calculation.

slides.say: So when is a table better? A table can hold a lot of data about the same groups.

slides: Here are the same three age groups. Now we also have children, friends, salary, and rooms at home.

slides.say: If a question needs one value, we just find it. At ages twenty-one to thirty, the salary is six thousand two hundred shekels.
The other columns don't bother us. We just ignore them.
at: The other columns don't bother us

slides.say: In a chart, so much data would be a mess. Too many lines or bars, and we can't see anything.
But a table has a weak point. To see a trend, we must read every number.
Look at the salary. Six thousand two hundred, then eight thousand three hundred, then ten thousand one hundred. It goes up with age.
And the friends go down. Twelve, nine, seven.
We had to read six numbers to see that. In a chart, we'd see one line going up and one going down, right away.
Now back to the practice tests. Here's another student. At the start the line is almost flat, so there's almost no improvement.
From the fifth test the line gets steep. From five to six, six to seven, seven to eight, the score goes up a lot.
at: the score goes up a lot

slides.say: Steeper means a bigger improvement. And from about the tenth test, it's flat again.
The dashed line is a third student. Almost nothing until the ninth test, and only then a sharp rise.

slides: By the way, the second student is the real picture for most of us. If your first practice tests don't improve, don't worry.

slides.say: The big jump usually comes from about the fourth or fifth test. Then the score levels off.

slides: That's it for the introduction. In the next lessons we'll go through each type of chart. I'll see you in the next video.
